# Sending Logs to Amazon S3

Logs published directly to Amazon S3 go to an existing bucket that you specify. One or more log files are created every five minutes in that bucket. When you set logs to be sent to Amazon S3, AWS creates or changes the resource policies associated with the receiving bucket, if needed.

The first time you deliver logs to an S3 bucket, the service that delivers logs records the bucket's owner, so that logs are delivered only to a bucket belonging to this account. To change the bucket owner, you must re-create or update the log subscription in the originating service.

## Required permissions

To set up sending logs to Amazon S3 for the first time, you must be logged into an account with the logs:CreateLogDelivery, S3:GetBucketPolicy, and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions. If any of these types of logs is already being sent to an S3 bucket, then to set up another of these log types for the same bucket you only need the logs:CreateLogDelivery permission.

## Bucket resource policy

The destination bucket must have a resource policy that includes certain permissions. How that policy gets created depends on the bucket's current state, and in both cases the user setting up logging must have the S3:GetBucketPolicy and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions:

- If the bucket has no resource policy, AWS automatically creates the log delivery policy when you begin sending logs to Amazon S3.
- If the bucket has a resource policy that doesn't contain the log delivery statement, that statement is appended to the existing policy.

Within the policy, aws:SourceAccount specifies the list of account IDs for which logs are being delivered to this bucket. aws:SourceArn specifies the list of ARNs of the resource that generates the logs, in the form arn:aws:logs:source-region:source-account-id:*.

If the bucket policy contains a NotAction or NotPrincipal element, automatically adding log delivery permissions and creating a log subscription will fail. In that case, you must manually add the log delivery permissions to the bucket policy and then create the log subscription.

AccessDenied errors may appear in AWS CloudTrail if the s3:ListBucket permission has not been granted to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com. To avoid them, grant s3:ListBucket to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com and include the Condition parameters shown with the s3:GetBucketAcl permission.

## CloudFront

CloudFront uses a different permissions model than the other services that send vended logs to S3. If you use the same S3 bucket for CloudFront access logs and another log source, enabling ACL on the bucket for CloudFront also grants permission to all other log sources that use that bucket.

## Encryption

You can protect the data in your S3 bucket by enabling either SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS.

- **SSE-S3:** No additional configuration is required.
- **SSE-KMS:** You must use a customer managed key, because an AWS managed key is not supported for this scenario. If you set up encryption using an AWS managed key, the logs will be delivered in an unreadable format.

When the bucket uses server-side encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must also add the key policy for that key. The required statement goes in the key policy for your customer managed key, not in the bucket policy for your S3 bucket, so that the log delivery account can write to your bucket. Note that if the destination bucket has SSE-KMS with a Bucket Key enabled, the attached customer managed KMS key policy no longer works as expected for all requests. Finally, if you're using vended logs and S3 encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must use a fully qualified AWS KMS key ARN rather than a key ID when you configure the bucket.

# Sending logs to Amazon S3

Logs published directly to Amazon S3 go to an existing bucket that you specify. One or more log files are created every five minutes in that bucket. When you set logs to be sent to Amazon S3, AWS creates or changes the resource policies associated with the receiving bucket, if needed.

The first time you deliver logs to an S3 bucket, the service that delivers logs records the bucket's owner. This ensures that logs are delivered only to a bucket belonging to this account. To change the bucket owner later, you must re-create or update the log subscription in the originating service.

CloudFront uses a different permissions model than the other services that send vended logs to S3. If you use the same S3 bucket for CloudFront access logs and for another log source, enabling ACL on the bucket for CloudFront also grants permission to all other log sources that use that bucket.

## Required user permissions

To set up sending logs to Amazon S3 for the first time, you must be logged into an account with the logs:CreateLogDelivery, S3:GetBucketPolicy, and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions. If any of these types of logs is already being sent to an S3 bucket, then to set up another of these log types to the same bucket you only need the logs:CreateLogDelivery permission.

## Bucket resource policy

The S3 bucket receiving the logs must have a resource policy that includes certain permissions. The policy is handled differently depending on its current state, and on whether the user setting up logging has the S3:GetBucketPolicy and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions for the bucket:

- If the bucket has no resource policy and the user has those permissions, AWS automatically creates the log delivery policy when you begin sending logs to S3.
- If the bucket has a resource policy that doesn't contain the log delivery statement and the user has those permissions, the statement is appended to the bucket's resource policy.

If the bucket policy contains a NotAction or NotPrincipal element, adding the log delivery permissions automatically and creating a log subscription will fail. In that case, to create the log subscription successfully, you must first manually add the log delivery permissions to the bucket policy, and then create the log subscription.

In the policy, aws:SourceAccount specifies the list of account IDs for which logs are being delivered to this bucket. aws:SourceArn specifies the list of ARNs of the resource that generates the logs, in the form arn:aws:logs:source-region:source-account-id:*.

AccessDenied errors may appear in AWS CloudTrail if the s3:ListBucket permission has not been granted to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com. To avoid these errors, you must grant s3:ListBucket to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com and include the Condition parameters shown with the s3:GetBucketAcl permission.

## Encrypting the bucket

You can protect the data in your S3 bucket by enabling either SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS.

- **SSE-S3:** No additional configuration is required.
- **SSE-KMS:** You must use a customer managed key, because using an AWS managed key is not supported for this scenario. If you set up encryption using an AWS managed key, the logs will be delivered in an unreadable format.

When using a customer managed KMS key, you must add the required statement to the key policy for your customer managed key, not to the bucket policy for your S3 bucket, so that the log delivery account can write to your S3 bucket. In other words, if the bucket has server-side encryption using a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must also add the key policy for that key.

Two further caveats apply to customer managed keys. If the destination bucket has SSE-KMS and a Bucket Key enabled, the attached customer managed KMS key policy no longer works as expected for all requests. And if you're using vended logs and S3 encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must use a fully qualified AWS KMS key ARN instead of a key ID when you configure the bucket.

## Sending logs to Amazon S3

Logs published directly to Amazon S3 are published to an existing bucket that you specify. One or more log files are created every five minutes in the specified bucket. When you set logs to be sent to Amazon S3, AWS creates or changes the resource policies associated with the S3 bucket that is receiving the logs, if needed.

When you deliver logs for the first time to an Amazon S3 bucket, the service that delivers logs records the owner of the bucket to ensure that the logs are delivered only to a bucket belonging to this account. Because the owner is recorded at that point, changing the bucket owner later requires that you re-create or update the log subscription in the originating service.

### Required permissions

To set up sending logs to Amazon S3 for the first time, you must be logged into an account with the logs:CreateLogDelivery, S3:GetBucketPolicy, and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions. If any of these types of logs is already being sent to an Amazon S3 bucket, then to set up the sending of another one of these types of logs to the same bucket you only need the logs:CreateLogDelivery permission.

### Bucket resource policy

The S3 bucket where the logs are being sent must have a resource policy that includes certain permissions. If the bucket currently does not have a resource policy and the user setting up the logging has the S3:GetBucketPolicy and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions for the bucket, AWS automatically creates the log delivery policy for it when you begin sending the logs to Amazon S3. This holds only when the user has all of the permissions required for first-time setup: logs:CreateLogDelivery, S3:GetBucketPolicy, and S3:PutBucketPolicy. If the bucket has a resource policy that doesn't contain the log delivery statement and the user has the S3:GetBucketPolicy and S3:PutBucketPolicy permissions, that statement is appended to the bucket's resource policy.

In the policy, aws:SourceAccount specifies the list of account IDs for which logs are being delivered to this bucket. aws:SourceArn specifies the list of ARNs of the resource that generates the logs, in the form arn:aws:logs:source-region:source-account-id:*.

If the bucket policy contains a NotAction or NotPrincipal element, adding log delivery permissions to the bucket automatically and creating a log subscription will fail. To create a log subscription successfully in this case, you need to manually add the log delivery permissions to the bucket policy, then create the log subscription.

AccessDenied errors may appear in AWS CloudTrail if the s3:ListBucket permission has not been granted to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com. To avoid these errors, you must grant the s3:ListBucket permission to delivery.logs.amazonaws.com and include the Condition parameters shown with the s3:GetBucketAcl permission.

### CloudFront

CloudFront uses a different permissions model than the other services that send vended logs to S3. If you use the same S3 bucket for CloudFront access logs and another log source, enabling ACL on the bucket for CloudFront also grants permission to all other log sources that use this bucket.

### Encryption

You can protect the data in your S3 bucket by enabling either SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS. These are alternatives, and the two options cannot both apply to the same configuration. If you choose SSE-S3, no additional configuration is required. If you choose SSE-KMS, you must use a customer managed key, because using an AWS managed key is not supported for this scenario. If you set up encryption using an AWS managed key, the logs will be delivered in an unreadable format, so an AWS managed key cannot be used and a customer managed key is required.

Because SSE-KMS requires a customer managed key, when using a customer managed KMS key you must add the required statement to the key policy for your customer managed key, not to the bucket policy for your S3 bucket, so that the log delivery account can write to your S3 bucket. If the bucket has server-side encryption using a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must also add the key policy for your customer managed key.

If the destination bucket has SSE-KMS and a Bucket Key enabled, the attached customer managed KMS key policy no longer works as expected for all requests. If you're using vended logs and S3 encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key, you must use a fully qualified AWS KMS key ARN instead of a key ID when you configure the bucket.
